questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 with a mark at every tenth, so it has 10 equal parts. Owen puts four counters on it: one on 0.4, one on 0.25 (halfway between the 0.2 and 0.3 marks), one on 3/10, and one on 0.9. Which counter is farthest to the RIGHT?
questions.explain: Farther right on the number line means greater, so compare tenths first: 0.9 is 9 tenths, more than 0.4, 3/10 (also 0.3) and 0.25. The common trap is picking 0.25 because it has more digits, but 0.25 is only 2 tenths and 5 hundredths.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is divided into 8 equal parts, so the marks are 1/8, 2/8, 3/8 and so on. Nadia puts one counter on 1/8 (the 1st mark), one on 1/4 (the 2nd mark) and one on 1/2 (the 4th mark). Which counter is closest to 0?
options: all three are the same distance from 0
questions.explain: On a line cut into 8 equal parts, 1/8 is only one part from 0, while 1/4 is two parts and 1/2 is four parts, so the one on 1/8 is closest to 0. The trap is thinking a bigger denominator makes a bigger fraction — with the same numerator, more parts means each part is smaller.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 with a mark at every tenth: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, all the way to 0.9. Which number belongs BETWEEN the 0.3 mark and the 0.4 mark?
questions.explain: Between 3 tenths and 4 tenths you need 3 tenths plus some hundredths, and 0.35 is 3 tenths and 5 hundredths. The trap is choosing 0.25 because 25 looks large, but 0.25 is only 2 tenths and 5 hundredths, so it sits to the left of the 0.3 mark.

questions.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 with a mark at every tenth, and the middle mark is labelled with the benchmark 1/2. Which of these numbers belongs to the RIGHT of the 1/2 mark?
questions.explain: The benchmark 1/2 is 0.5, so compare each number with 0.5: 5/8 is 0.625, which is past the middle mark, while 0.45, 2/5 (0.4) and 0.4 all land before it. The trap is thinking 0.45 is past 0.5 because 45 is bigger than 5 — 0.45 is 4 tenths and 5 hundredths, less than 5 tenths.

questions.question: Lin, Marco and Ava check the rain gauge in the school garden. Lin records 0.4 cm, Marco records 0.35 cm and Ava records 3/8 cm. They want to place all three on a number line from 0 cm to 1 cm. Which order is least to greatest?
questions.explain: Change 3/8 to a decimal (3 divided by 8 is 0.375), then order: 0.35, then 0.375, then 0.4. Two traps to avoid: thinking 0.35 is bigger than 0.4 because it has more digits, and thinking 3/8 is the largest because 8 is the biggest denominator.

questions.question: Mika is marking a number line from 0 to 1 to show how full the class recycling bin is. The bin is more than 1/2 full but less than 3/4 full. Which decimal could show how full the bin is?
questions.explain: The benchmarks 1/2 and 3/4 are 0.5 and 0.75, so the number must sit between 0.5 and 0.75, and 0.6 does. Watch the trap of picking 0.45: extra digits do not make a decimal larger, and 0.45 is less than 0.5, so it lands left of the halfway mark.

questions.question: At Sports Day, four students record their long jumps: Aiden 2.05 m, Sara 1.75 m, Tomas 1 4/5 m and Priya 1.9 m. To place them on a number line from 1 m to 3 m, which order is least to greatest?
questions.explain: Write 1 4/5 as 1.8, then order by tenths: 1.75, 1.8, 1.9, 2.05. The usual trap is treating 1.75 as the biggest because it has the most digits, but 1.75 is 7 tenths and 5 hundredths, so it sits left of 1.8.

questions.question: Five students measure the snow depth on the school field and get 0.3 m, 1/4 m, 0.45 m, 2/5 m and 0.5 m. They place all five on a number line and then find the median, the middle value. What is the median depth?
questions.explain: Change the fractions to decimals (1/4 is 0.25 and 2/5 is 0.4), order them on the line as 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5, and the middle one is 0.4, which is 2/5. The trap is taking the middle of the list as written (0.45) instead of ordering first.

questions.question: Kai is placing numbers on a class number line and says: 'On the line, 0.25 goes to the right of 0.3, because 25 is bigger than 3.' Which statement fixes Kai's thinking?
options: 0.25 is 2 tenths and 5 hundredths, which is less than 3 tenths, so it goes to the LEFT of 0.3
Kai is right — hundredths are worth more than tenths, so 0.25 goes to the right of 0.3
0.25 and 0.3 land on the same point, since 0.25 rounds to 0.3 when you keep only one decimal place
Kai is right — 0.25 has more digits than 0.3, so it is the greater number and goes to the right
questions.explain: Compare place value from the left: 0.25 has 2 tenths and 0.3 has 3 tenths, so 0.25 is smaller and sits left of 0.3 (think 0.30 versus 0.25). A longer decimal is not automatically bigger — the digits after the point are smaller and smaller pieces.

questions.question: Nora is putting fraction cards on a number line from 0 to 1. She says 1/8 goes to the right of 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4. Which statement is correct?
options: Nora is right: 1/8 sits between 1/4 and 1/2
1/8 sits between 0 and 1/4, so 1/4 is the greater fraction
1/8 and 1/4 sit on exactly the same point
Nora is right: 1/8 sits to the right of the 1/2 benchmark
questions.explain: Cutting a whole into 8 parts makes smaller pieces than cutting it into 4, so one eighth lands between 0 and 1/4 (using equivalent fractions, 1/4 is 2/8). The trap is reading the bigger denominator as the bigger fraction when the numerators are the same.

questions.question: In cooking class, Priya pours 0.6 L of water, Devon pours 5/8 L and Mei pours 0.55 L. They mark all three amounts on a number line from 0 L to 1 L. Who poured the most, and who poured the least?
options: Priya poured the most, Mei poured the least
Mei poured the most, Devon poured the least
Devon poured the most, Mei poured the least
Devon poured the most, Priya poured the least
questions.explain: First change 5/8 to 0.625, then order on the line: 0.55, 0.6, 0.625, so Devon is farthest right and Mei is farthest left. The trap is thinking 0.55 beats 0.6 because it has more digits — 0.6 is the same as 0.60, which is greater than 0.55.

questions.question: The class is building a number line from 2 to 3 for the math wall. They have four cards: 2.05, 2 1/8, 2.5 and 2 3/4. Which card goes closest to the whole number 2?
questions.explain: Find how far past 2 each card is: 0.05, then 1/8 which is 0.125, then 0.5, then 0.75 — so 2.05 sits nearest the whole number 2. Two traps: thinking 2.05 is far from 2 because of the extra digit, and thinking 1/8 is a large jump because 8 is a big denominator.
